# SK5021 — An RSA or DSA key generated below 2048 bits

<!-- Generated from Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/rules.json. Do not edit. -->

A 1024-bit RSA or DSA modulus is a budget away from being factored, and the size is written at the call.

| | |
|---|---|
| Category | Security |
| Default severity | error |
| Scope | Semantic |
| Needs a compilation | yes |
| Fix | yes, review it |
| Language version floor | — |
| Since | 2.0 |
| Supersedes | S4426 |

## Why

The security of RSA and of finite-field DSA is the cost of factoring a number that the code chooses the size of, and that cost has been falling for forty years while the number stayed the same length. A 1024-bit modulus is estimated at about 80 bits of work; NIST SP 800-57 has required 112 bits — which is 2048 — since 2014, and CA/Browser Forum rules stopped issuing certificates below it at the same time. The distance between "nobody has published a 1024-bit factorisation" and "nobody can afford one" is not a security property, and it is not the sort of thing to find out about afterwards, because a key that turns out to be factorable retroactively invalidates every signature it ever made. The size is a single argument at the generation call, which is what makes this decidable where most cryptographic mistakes are not. Generate at least 2048 bits — or move to `ECDsa`, where a 256-bit key is stronger than a 3072-bit RSA one, the keys and signatures are an order of magnitude smaller, and generation is fast enough to do per-request.

## Example

Instead of:

```csharp
using var signer = RSA.Create(1024);
var signature = signer.SignData(payload, HashAlgorithmName.SHA256, RSASignaturePadding.Pkcs1);
```

Write:

```csharp
using var signer = RSA.Create(2048);
var signature = signer.SignData(payload, HashAlgorithmName.SHA256, RSASignaturePadding.Pkcs1);
```

## When it does not fire

⚠ **The SDK covers exactly one spelling of this and it is the legacy one, which is the whole argument for the rule.** Measured on a plain `net10.0` project outside this repository under `-p:AnalysisMode=All`, so the analyzers demonstrably ran: `CA5385` fires on `new RSACryptoServiceProvider(1024)` and on **nothing else** — not on `RSA.Create(1024)`, which is the modern factory and the spelling every current sample uses; not on `DSA.Create(1024)`; and not on `rsa.KeySize = 1024` even where `rsa` is an `RSACryptoServiceProvider`, the very type `CA5385`'s own message names. `CA5384` reports `DSACryptoServiceProvider` as an algorithm regardless of its key size and likewise misses `DSA.Create`. Both are off by default. ⚠ **Elliptic curves are excluded deliberately rather than overlooked.** `KeySize` is declared on `AsymmetricAlgorithm`, whose other descendants are `ECDsa` and `ECDiffieHellman`, where 256 bits is *stronger* than 2048-bit RSA — so the family test is on the receiver's type and reaches only `RSA` and `DSA`. A bit-count floor applied across algorithm families would make this rule report the replacement it recommends. ⚠ **Only a compile-time-constant size**, so a key size read from configuration is silence rather than a guess, and only a positive one, so a sentinel is not reported as a weak key. ⚠ **Test code is exempt**, by the shared test six other rules use — the enclosing method's attribute, or the enclosing type holding a test case, which is what reaches a fixture's constructor and teardown ([#319]): generating a deliberately small key to keep a test fast is real and correct, and a security rule at `error` that breaks a test suite teaches a reviewer to skim past every security finding the tool makes. ⚠ **`fixIsSafe: false`, and the fix is still carried.** Raising the argument to 2048 compiles, binds and is strictly stronger, but the size is half of an agreement with whoever holds the other end of the protocol; a tool that changed it silently under `--fix` would be renegotiating that agreement on its own authority. ⚠ **The reference trees prove nothing here and the zero is reported as such**: no file under `Testing/corpus` mentions `System.Security.Cryptography`, so the corpus zero is *shape absent*, not *correctly declined*.
